title: Damien Aubin Documents a Former Soviet Mining Settlement Suspended in Time
description: The small settlement of Pyramiden on the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard is literally frozen in time. A former mining outpost for the Soviet Uni
body:
The small settlement of Pyramiden on the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard is literally frozen in time. A former mining outpost for the Soviet Union, industrial operations ceased in 1998, and residents relocated. It wasn’t until 2007 that a handful of new inhabitants made the settlement home.
Because Pyramiden was abandoned in a cold climate, it remains impeccably preserved, with remnants of its once-thriving settlement still visible. French photographer Damien Aubin visited the Arctic region and documented the still, serene environment blanketed in snow. “The place has not been abandoned. It has been left in suspension,” he says. 
Classroom, Pyramiden
Pyramiden’s buildings and the objects inside are largely unchanged. Books sit open on school desks, and an unblemished statue of Lenin presides over a common area. Outside, a towering outdoor monument soars into the sky, the vibrant red and blue paint a stark contrast to the otherwise white landscape. 
“I photograph these environments at a distance, in a restrained, diffuse light. There is no event to describe, no narrative to unfold,” Aubin adds. “Across Pyramiden, Barentsburg and Longyearbyen, the same condition appears:spaces shaped by human intent, no longer aligned with it.”
Aubin has compiled the photos in a limited-edition book slated for release in September. You can purchase a copy on his website.

title: Trump Installs Thomas Jefferson Statue in the Rose Garden
description:
Trump Administration
                The artist behind the piece is also responsible for a MAGA-friendly Trump statue.
body:
Trump Administration
                The artist behind the piece is also responsible for a MAGA-friendly Trump statue. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            The Thomas Jefferson statue from sculptor George Lundeen's home in Loveland, Colorado. (Courtesy George Lundeen).President Donald Trump continues to furnish the White House Rose Garden with statues of his favorite predecessors, most recently adding a bronze of the third US President, Thomas Jefferson. Made by Colorado-based artist George Lundeen, the statue portrays the founding father seated on a bench with a quill in his hand and the Declaration of Independence on his lap. He looks into the distance, as if he's pausing to ponder while authoring the historical document. The Jefferson piece marks the fifth addition to Trump's Rose Garden, which already contains sculptures of George Washington, Alexander Hamilton, Benjamin Franklin, and "Freedom's Charge" — a statue depicting two Revolutionary War soldiers.In a statement to Hyperallergic, Lundeen said that he had completed the statue 25 years ago. "Without Thomas Jefferson, you have to wonder whether there would be a United States of America," he said.The artist also collaborated on a statue of the president holding a "Make America Great Again" hat and pumping the air with his fist — a posture meant to capture Trump's reaction immediately after the 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania. That piece now resides in Trump's golf club in West Palm Beach, Florida.  Implementing the Jefferson statue is one of Trump's latest efforts to reshape the White House Grounds and DC at large. Since renovations to the Rose Garden began in 2020, Trump has razed the Kennedy-Era Lawn in favor of a Mar-a-Lago-style patio, and installed a "Presidential Walk of Fame" with portraits of all US presidents except for Joe Biden, who was sarcastically replaced with an autopen device.Trump's aesthetic aims extend to other parts of the capital city. In June, six heritage preservation groups based in Washington, DC, sued the Trump administration over its plans to create a "Garden of American Heroes" in West Potomac Park. The garden is meant to include 250 American heroes, from Muhammad Ali and Frederick Douglass, to divisive figures like Christopher Columbus, whose likeness made an earlier appearance in the White House compound in March.

title: Nvidia CEO Pours $75M Into San Francisco Art Campus
description:
News
                Vanderbilt University's building on the ruins of the California College of the Arts will bear the billionai
body:
News
                Vanderbilt University's building on the ruins of the California College of the Arts will bear the billionaire's name   
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang on January 5, 2026 (photo Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
    
        
            Vanderbilt University's new San Francisco arts and design campus will bear the name of Nvidia co-founder Jensen (Jen-Hsun) Huang after the billionaire committed millions to the institution. The university announced this week that the AI chipmaker and his wife, Lori Huang, gifted $75 million to establish the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design.The controversial campus will replace the nearly 120-year-old California College of the Arts (CCA), San Francisco's last remaining private art school. The beloved nonprofit institution, which grants bachelor's and master's degrees across artistic disciplines, was purchased by Vanderbilt amid financial struggles caused by a decline in enrollment and a growing budget deficit.The Huangs donated a $22.5 million matching gift to CCA in February 2025 to help stabilize the institution's shaky finances. However, not even a full year later, CCA announced that it would cease operating after the 2026–2027 academic year, and that the Potrero Hill campus would be subsumed by Vanderbilt. Not everyone in the local art community is happy with Huang's donation. "These billionaires would much rather play God and remake our art schools in their own image than support a 120-year-old legacy fine art school," Lindsey White, a San Francisco-based artist, educator, and CCA alum, told Hyperallergic."In both CCA and SFAI cases, billionaires with zero experience in the arts have taken over major real estate, leaving local artists, educators, and workers in a dystopian nightmare," White continued. "Sadly, it seems our local government didn't see the value in saving the last fine art school in Northern California either."California Governor Gavin Newsom had worked to secure a $20 million public grant in 2025 to keep the private institution afloat despite significant opposition from state lawmakers. At the time, the governor argued that though it was atypical for the government to fund a private college, the state should fund CCA to safeguard its cultural sector amid Trump's attacks on the arts. He later expressed shock at the school's closure, but critics said he should've seen it coming. Huang co-founded Nvidia, a manufacturer of graphics processing units (GPUs) now widely used to power artificial intelligence programs, in a Denny's restaurant booth in 1993. In May, the chipmaker reached a valuation of $5.5 trillion, the highest in the history of publicly traded companies. According to the university's announcement, the Huangs donated the large sum out of their belief that "creative practice [is] one of innovation’s most essential engines."“Technology expands what we can build," Jensen Huang said in the press release issued earlier this week. "Art and design determine why we build it. Together they shape civilization."In an op-ed about the closure of CCA in the San Francisco Chronicle earlier this year, local gallerist Griff Williams warned that "corporate interests seem to eclipse all else in San Francisco.""Mayor Lurie, the closure of the California College of the Arts is a tragedy for the city, not a 'win,'" he wrote. "It’s another blow to the legacy of the heroes who made San Francisco unique: Joan Brown, David Ireland, Bruce Conner, Hung Liu, Hank Willis Thomas, Dewey Crumpler, Robert Arneson, Manuel Neri, Harrell Fletcher, Jim Goldberg, Viola Frey, Ted Purves, Dodie Bellamy and Susan O’Malley, to name a few."

title: Joyce Kozloff Reveals Herself as  Guerrilla Girls Founding Member
description:
News
                After decades of anonymity, the feminist artist and activist disclosed in an interview that she is the woman beh
body:
News
                After decades of anonymity, the feminist artist and activist disclosed in an interview that she is the woman behind the mask of “Liubov Popova.” 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Joyce Kozloff attends the opening reception for Local Editions: Prints by New York Artists (2018) at the Metropolitan Museum of Art (photo Taylor Hill via Getty Images)Artist and activist Joyce Kozloff has taken off the mask after 41 years, disclosing in a new interview with Art Journal Open that she was among the founding members of the Guerrilla Girls. She also revealed that “Liubov Popova” was her assigned pseudonym within the collective, whose members took the names of late women artists to maintain their own anonymity. In 2016, she published a (sneaky) biographical essay in Hyperallergic that both examined and lauded the Russian artist's creative evolution and career milestones throughout her unfortunately short life. “Remaining anonymous was an important Guerrilla Girls decision,” Kozloff explained to curators Maura Reilly and Helena Reckitt during her tell-all in the American magazine's Feminist Interview Project. “People thought this was to avoid art world reprisals. For me, that was never the reason. I argued for anonymity because I didn’t want attention to be on us as individuals, I wanted it to remain on the issues.”The artist said that she and two others were among the seven inaugural Guerrilla Girls who had lived through the women's movement in the 1970s, and that the younger women in the collective proclaimed that people had become disinterested with feminism, outlining a need for updated language and visuals. Having moved to Los Angeles when her husband Max began teaching at the California Institute of the Arts, Kozloff joined a feminist “consciousness raising” group that quickly radicalized her in 1971. This experience gave way to her role in co-organizing the Los Angeles Council of Women Artists (LACWA) that protested the paucity of female representation at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.Kozloff's role in the feminist art movement expanded upon her return to New York in the early '70s — she was among the inaugural members of the Heresies Collective, and her art practice and shift to public art bolstered the emerging Pattern and Decoration movement.LACWA's data-driven protest model laid the basic framework for the Guerrilla Girls, which got its name after a new member misunderstood the title and brought a (now signature) gorilla mask to a meeting. Among the group's debut interventions was an ad campaign calling out the disparity between the number of women artists shown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art versus the number of displayed artworks depicting nude women.The group's confrontational wheat-pasted posters directly named and shamed institutions, galleries, and collectors that maintained sexist and racist hierarchies, drawing immense publicity and curiosity about the Guerrilla Girls' identities. “People were pissed and wanted to out us,” Kozloff told Reckitt and Reilly, adding that she was affiliated with the Guerrilla Girls until 1991. A printed reproduction of the Guerrilla Girls' “The Advantages of Being a Woman Artist” (1988) at the 2018 Gowanus Open Studios (photo Alissa Guzman/Hyperallergic)The artist also revealed her hand in developing one of the collective's most iconic poster campaigns — “The Advantages of Being a Woman Artist” (1988). She told Art Journal Open that the project was born from her time in a residency house she shared with married male artists who had brought their younger affair partners along as homemakers and unpaid studio assistants.“When I got back, I wrote a rough draft, 'The Disadvantages of Being a Woman Artist,'” Kozloff explained. “Until then, our posters always had verifiable statistics, so this was a stretch. But then, our clever members turned it around to 'Advantages,' and it worked!”Four decades on, Kozloff thinks that there has been enormous progress in the representation of women in the arts sphere. But, she said, “I'm very much more concerned about the current threats to women’s progress in the larger political realm,” citing the overturning of Roe v. Wade, the far-right push to keep women at home, and the beauty industry's invasive emphasis on youthful appearances.“But we can’t tell the next generation what to do, they will find their own ways,” she left off.

title: Sable Elyse Smith Reveals the Shapes of State Violence
description:
Art Review
                The artist’s critique of the prison-industrial complex simultaneously deepens and skewers the legacie
body:
Art Review
                The artist’s critique of the prison-industrial complex simultaneously deepens and skewers the legacies of Minimalism.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Sable Elyse Smith, “Coloring Book 111” (2022), screen printing ink, oil stick, and oil pastel on paper (all photos Liz Kim/Hyperallergic)AUSTIN — A sustained critique of the United States carceral system runs through Sable Elyse Smith's work. Clockwork at the Contemporary Austin, the culmination of her winning the 2026 Suzanne Deal Booth / FLAG Art Foundation Prize, consists mainly of paintings appropriating prison coloring books for visiting children on the first floor, and large-scale sculptures and installations on the second. Seen as a whole, Smith’s work co-opts Minimalism’s repetition and seriality as a metaphor for structural injustice, drawing attention to the rhythmic qualities of technological and administrative tyranny. The coloring books Smith adapts were originally created to help children emotionally absorb the violence of incarceration. Smith’s transformations seem to liquefact their pictures and texts so that they melt the foundations of the institutions they represent. Two works share the same page design, a waiting room of a courthouse filled with families as well as an assortment of creatures, asking — absurdly — “What 10 things don’t belong in this picture?” One version of Smith’s coloring scheme blocks in a select number of the human figures in solid blue, turning them into police officers as omnipotent institutional authority, while the other version places x’s and o’s across figures and faces, referencing the oppressiveness of such spaces. Smith rightly shifts the ludicrous question of belonging into a critique of recurrent power structures. Left: Sable Elyse Smith, “Coloring Book 117” (2023), screen printing ink, oil pastel, oil stick, and wax pencil on paper; right: Sable Elyse Smith, “BARRICADE” (2023), powder-coated aluminumSmith’s two videos fit like gloves together. “LAUGH TRACK, OR WHO’S THAT PEEKING IN MY WINDOW” (2021) is a series of footage appropriated from police reality TV shows, which are repeatedly rewound, fast-forwarded, and shown upside down. One sequence captures a routine traffic enforcement for a rolling stop that turns into a state-sanctioned detention without cause — under the pretense of an unrelated previous conviction, a police officer stops a vehicle and frisks its passenger, places him in cuffs, and takes pictures of his face and his back tattoos. A repeated xylophone noise draws attention to those moments when socially conditioned biases and bureaucratic procedures trigger state violence. Through the use of repetition in both footage and sound, Smith emphasizes the aggressive and senseless criminal profiling of an innocent person by juxtaposing Minimalism’s iterative assault against reality television’s numbing effects.In the adjacent “skin suit” (2025), law enforcement deals first with young White men. One sequence shows an officer finding drug and alcohol paraphernalia, along with a mask, a realistic pellet gun, gloves, and large knives contained in a bag in the trunk. After these extensive discoveries, the officer lets the person go, while giving him a fist bump. Afterward, another young White man is shown agitating an officer outside the open window of his patrol vehicle before the latter patiently drives away. This is juxtaposed with footage of a young Black man being held against his will due to the possession of marijuana. As the narrator later states, this video is about “bags of skin,” because “there are no people here” — the carceral system, Smith suggests, abstracts individuals entirely.  Smith’s sculptures are made of chairs and tables from prisons that are meant to be permanently drilled into the floor, rendered immovable like the institutions they represent. Their weaponization by the state is apparent in their rigidity, as tools that force imprisoned people into geometric configurations to better surveil them. This critique of the prison-industrial complex simultaneously deepens and skewers the legacies of Minimalism — one cannot help but think of Frank Stella’s polygons while surrounded by Smith’s work. Only, one also can’t help but notice the impotence of formal precision without larger social critique. Sable Elyse Smith, “BACKBEND” (2019), powder-coated aluminumSable Elyse Smith, “A Clockwork” (2021), aluminum, steel, and motorInstallation view of Sable Elyse Smith, “LAUGH TRACK, OR WHO’S THAT PEEKING IN MY WINDOW” (2021), high-definition video, color, and sound, 7:56 minutesInstallation view of Sable Elyse Smith: ClockworkSable Elyse Smith: Clockwork continues at the Contemporary Austin (3809 West 35th Street, Austin, Texas) through August 2. The exhibition was curated by Alex Klein and Julie Le. The exhibition will travel to the FLAG Art Foundation in New York in September; that iteration will be curated by Jonathan Rider.

title: Emory Douglas’s Lifetime of Revolutionary Art
description:
Art Review
                At age 83, the former Black Panther Party culture minister continues to explore the possibilities of
body:
Art Review
                At age 83, the former Black Panther Party culture minister continues to explore the possibilities of unapologetically political art.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Emory Douglas, “Red White Blue Wickedness” (2025), digital archival print (image Max Blue/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            SAN FRANCISCO — Emory Douglas honed his craft in the trenches of political artmaking. The artist first learned the basics of commercial printing while serving a 15-month sentence at a juvenile correctional facility at the age of 13; later, he became the minister of culture for the Black Panther Party, where he designed the party’s newspaper and shaped the group’s political aesthetic. Douglas’s deep-seated understanding of the strength of printed material and critical eye toward oppressive power structures have remained key features of his work for decades. Now, the 83-year-old artist is the subject of the survey exhibition Emory Douglas: In Our Lifetime at San Francisco’s African American Art and Culture Complex, complete with paintings, prints, and political cartoons spanning decades and issues. It makes the case that to be a contemporary artist, one must remain politically engaged, ever navigating and responding to the times they live in.A large poster spelling out Douglas’s 12 commandments on making effective political art welcomes visitors into the exhibition. Among the bullet points in his “Political Artist Manifesto” are warnings like “Don’t be fooled by deception” and “Do not lose sight of what the goals are.” Others are more aspirational, such as “Create art that recognizes the oppression of others, and considers basic quality of life concerns and basic human rights issues,” or simply, “You get more truth from the artists than from bureaucrats.” Hung beneath the classic Black Panther Party logo of a prowling jungle cat, the list operates as a key text for the show, giving a clear sense of Douglas’s principled conceptual framework. In this day and age — and indeed, perhaps always — it is a document that more artists and arts organizations ought to read.Emory Douglas's "Political Artist Manifesto"A large selection of Douglas’s early political cartoons and posters from the late 1960s and ’70s offer entire worldviews in a single frame, from advertisements for the Black Panther Party’s People’s Free Food Program to indictments of greedy landlords and police brutality. In “38th Puppet of the United States” (1974), Gerald Ford is controlled like a marionette by a hand emblazoned with corporate logos. “Cointelpro” (1978) shows a Spy vs. Spy-like character clutching a smoking gun while surveying wanted-poster-style mugshots of Black revolutionaries. The print is titled for the FBI counterintelligence initiative under which multiple Black revolutionaries were assassinated, including Chicago Black Panther Party Chairman Fred Hampton.Sometimes Douglas does find humor, often at the expense of the state. “Whatever is good for the oppressor has got to be bad for us” (1968) shows humanoid pigs marching a group of Black people off of a pig-shaped rocket ship. In it, the United States’s histories of slavery and imperialism are deftly intertwined in a darkly humorous scene: One of the pigs overlooking the proceedings says, “Hey handle those slaves with care we’re gonna need them for Mars, Pluto and all the other planets.” One of the captives remarks, “I knew we should have stopped this shit before it got off the ground” — a punny reference to the rocket ship and the real-world evils it symbolizes. In an accompanying collage, “White Only” (2021), Donald Trump can be seen hammering the titular signage to the pigs’ rocket ship and saying “At last” — one of several instances in which Douglas uses old work to reflect on the present.Emory Douglas, "Whatever is good for the oppressor has got to be bad for us, Remix" (1969), archival print (left) and "White Only, Remix" (2021), digital archival print (right)In a world inundated with AI slop, Douglas makes the best case for digital art I’ve seen in recent years. He characterizes several of his digital illustrations as “remixes,” updating key elements and motifs from older, recognizable artworks to help them maintain present-day political relevance. Douglas also takes the opportunity to incorporate statements about issues beyond the Black American experience, including the Vietnam War, violence in Haiti, and the genocide in Palestine, emphasizing the global interconnectedness and reach of solidarity movements.Douglas remains determined to engage with ongoing political issues and adapt to the times, while presenting his signature illustrative style in both contemporary and traditional mediums. In the digital drawing “Ethnic Cleansing / GENOCIDE” (2026), a grieving woman holds an infant swaddled in the Palestinian flag. In the acrylic painting “Free the Land” (2010), a freedom fighter swathed in a keffiyeh against a striking yellow backdrop takes aim at an unseen enemy with a slingshot, a pose reminiscent of David battling Goliath or Susan Meiselas’s 1979 photograph of Nicaraguan revolutionary Pablo Arauz tossing a molotov cocktail. In the digital illustration “Red White Blue Wickedness” (2025), two faces separated by fencing weep against the backdrop of an American flag. The phrase “ICE cold wickedness” is printed at the top of the composition, “Made in the USA” at the bottom.Installation view of Emory Douglas: In Our LifetimeNot all of Douglas’s images of political unrest are images of strife. In several scenes, love is expressed through revolutionary community and acts of political education. In the brightly colored, graphic digital drawing “I Am We” (2018), a child wearing a Colin Kaepernick jersey and sporting a bold orange halo plays with a toy globe, while another child, smiling and raising their fist in the foreground, wears a pin that reads, “I am we.” In “Fight Sickle Cell Anemia,” a pen-and-ink infographic illustration from 1973, a parent reads to a child from a book of the same title. Family is often the site of solidarity and political education in Douglas’s work, with special attention paid to how the next generation will carry the political torch.Throughout In Our Lifetime, Douglas takes a refreshingly uncompromising orientation toward the kind of direct messaging that frequently gets scrubbed from art in favor of palatable, salable nuance. But Douglas isn’t interested in being palatable. He’s interested in articulating his political position as clearly as possible.In recent years, many San Francisco museums have struggled to meet the political moment head-on. In 2024, the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts closed its triennial Bay Area Now exhibition when artists altered their own work with pro-Palestinian messaging. The center has still not publicly addressed the incident, despite turnover in museum leadership. Later that same year, a group of pro-Palestine artists withdrew from the Contemporary Jewish Museum’s California Jewish Open, citing censorship of their work. The city’s larger museums, such as the de Young or the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA), have continued to mount blockbuster shows without much political — or artistic — merit, making a case for only one side of the equation: the bottom line.Installation view of Emory Douglas: In Our LifetimeIn 2021, Douglas’s text-based mural “Reparations” was installed at SFMOMA. While the work felt like a significant gesture on the museum’s part at the time, it’s hard not to see it as a platitude given the institution’s uneven track record on engaging with the current political moment. The small-scale vinyl of the piece included in In Our Lifetime, situated in the context of the African American Art and Culture Complex and Douglas’s other work, packs a stronger punch. Too many museums and arts organizations today seem to conveniently forget that, in Douglas’s words, “culture is a weapon.”Both SOMArts and the African American Art and Culture Complex, two of San Francisco’s city-funded cultural organizations, have mounted explicitly political exhibitions, highlighting work by Palestinian and pro-Palestine artists. Their shows are proof that during moments of political upheaval, maintaining financial freedom from corporate donors — whose politics inform the programming of the institutions they fund — pays off. During the current period of censorship at cultural institutions across the country, smaller, locally funded organizations are often better positioned than their major institutional counterparts to mount politically engaged shows. It’s a mode of hyperlocal politics in art and activism that other institutions ought to emulate — and one that Douglas is no stranger to. He helped create it.Emory Douglas: In Our Lifetime continues at the African American Art and Culture Complex (762 Fulton Street, San Francisco, California) through October 2026. The exhibition was organized by Rio Yañez and Rosalind McGary.

title: Christopher Nolan, David Hockney, Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara
description:
Weekly Newsletter
                A political prisoner is freed, a Homerist reviews Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” and do we have to pre
body:
Weekly Newsletter
                A political prisoner is freed, a Homerist reviews Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” and do we have to pretend to like David Hockney’s iPad paintings?
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            After five years in a maximum-security prison outside Havana, Cuban dissident artist Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara was released and exiled to Miami. He's a free man now, but there's not much to celebrate. The US continues to choke the island, driving its people into despair. Justice is scarce both here and there.Meanwhile, everyone's talking about Christopher Nolan's film adaptation of The Odyssey, so we got a certified Homerist to review the film for us. "As a spectacle, the movie is a fantastic success," writes Joel P. Christensen of CUNY Graduate Center. "As a reflection of us, it fails."Now to a delicate subject: the late David Hockney's iPad paintings. Yes, the tablet device allowed him to continue making art in his sunset years, but must we pretend to like the outcome even if we don't? Our London critic Olivia McEwan thinks not.Scroll down to read about the political message behind a giant wiener in Times Square, the short-spined raccoon that became the darling of misfits everywhere, and the intense backlash over a Hollywood star's pair of earrings. Thanks for reading. I think I'll go see The Odyssey this weekend.—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

	
		
			Zendaya’s Earrings Are Part of a Much Bigger Problem
		
	
	
		Zendaya faced backlash for wearing a pair of 3,000-year-old Iranian gold discs at a London photocall for Christopher Nolan’s forthcoming adaptation of The Odyssey earlier this month. The discs, mounted in 18-karat gold and diamonds, were recently made into earrings by jeweler Glenn Spiro as part of his Materials of the Old World collection, and subsequently acquired by London jewelry house Barron London, who stated that they are part of the company’s private collection and not for sale. However, they did not belong on the red carpet at all. 
      
Described as a “voracious collector,” mesmerized by special artifacts “regardless of their provenance,” Spiro said in an interview about the collection, “You can wear something around your neck that dates back thousands of years but is still contemporary and cool.” One online review of Spiro’s collection perfectly captures the performative exoticism driving this kind of repurposing: “... fragments of forgotten empires are not merely displayed but reborn.”
	
	
		Read More

            NewsThe Art Institute of Chicago plans to transfer its in-house custodial workforce to a private contractor in August, drawing outcry from unionized workers.Cuban dissident performance artist Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara arrived in Miami after over a week of ambiguity surrounding his whereabouts following his scheduled release from a five-year sentence for “contempt, defamation, and public disorder.”New York Chinatown residents and activists protested outside a town hall event at the Museum of Chinese in America, condemning the leadership’s acceptance of a $35 million grant from the city that they believe is tied to the construction of a borough jail.Following a legal battle between the city of Philadelphia and the Trump administration, federal officials replaced exhibits describing the history of slavery in the United States at a Pennsylvania historical park.  A newly shared letter reveals that alleged “racist” and “culturally insensitive” behaviors contributed to Yuko Kikuchi’s January resignation from her post as head of academic programs at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.Tate names Jessica Morgan, who led the Dia Art Foundation in New York for over a decade, as its next director.Two painters are suing The Hole Gallery, alleging that it owes them a combined sum of about $50,000 in outstanding sales proceeds.Collectors Anne and Arthur Goldstein gift over 70 works of modern and contemporary art to the Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers University.Dmitriy Popov was handed a 20-year sentence over the fatal stabbing of Black gay professional dancer O’Shae Sibley. The sentencing comes after Popov was convicted of manslaughter as a hate crime in June.Just weeks before a historic collection of 20th-century Mexican art is slated to leave the country for an exhibition in Europe, a group of advocates is suing Mexico’s principal cultural entity over allegations regarding the legal basis for exporting the nation’s artistic heritage.Just a few months after the reopening of the New Museum’s expanded building, a water leak shut down the Manhattan institution for a full weekend.The New York Foundation for the Arts awards $903,000 to 132 artists across New York State in its joint fellowship program with the New York State Council on the Arts.Art Movements: Michael Wellen and José Luis Blondet are the curators of the next Made in L.A., Tate names a new director, and the Immigrant Artist Biennial is back for another edition.

			The Sunflower Effect of Kyung-Me
